author: boazbaraktcs
text:

This classical view doesn't always hold, even in physics and crypto. Also, some people mix theory&practice (in a different universe, bitcoin could have been two papers: one on theory and one on implementation)

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @doschroeder @kennyog Maybe the terms "ahead" or "behind" are not the right ones. I wanted to contrast a different dynamic between crypto in machine learning. The classical view of theory is that, because it's not tethered to practical considerations, it can move faster in exploring what's possible.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
We want to come up with hypotheses clean enough to be informative, and precise enough to be refutable.

It is absolutely OK, as @tomgoldsteincs says, to be wrong. The danger we should watch out for is that we not become so vague in our hypotheses that we're "not even wrong".

author: boazbaraktcs
text: So, if we want to gain understanding, mathematical theorems are one tool in our belt, but we can and should also reach for others, drawing inspiration from natural sciences.  These include not just theorems but also (and maybe mostly) observations and experiments.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
..we have practical tools that exhibit too complex a behavior for us to analyze with our theoretical tools.

In that sense, these tools behave more similar to discovered natural objects than to designed algorithms.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
They were proposed in 80s and 90s, considered wildly impractical, and only recently began to be implemented and used.

In contrast, in deep learning currently, practice is ahead of theory. Rather than having theoretical proposals that are too complex or inefficient to implement..

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias Btw it seems that you agree with @mattyglesias ‘s original Tweet, but your main argument is that we should change the way we treat flu to be like Covid rather than the other way around. 

https://t.co/bjVmPB2W5G

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I would guess that at the moment a large fraction, possibly a majority, of the Covid positive kids currently in isolation are both feeling fine and actually not infectious. Often by the time you get tested and get the results, much of the infectious period is over.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I definitely agree that if you know for sure a kid *will* infect a classmate if they go to school then they should stay home. But often you could test positive (esp with PCR) at the tail end when you’re no longer infectious.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I guess the question is reduces the chance by how much and what’s the conditional probability for a (vaxxed&boosted) kid to get sick of they do catch it. It seems the latter is lower for Covid than the flu.  I don’t know the answer to this calculation but it’s not obvious to me.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I’m really sorry to hear that. I would have hoped that masking etc would at least keep kids from getting the flu. 

These respiratory diseases are all quite nasty, and I do hope that improved ventilation and more comfort with masks will reduce their prevalence in the future.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias By “enforce” I mean that if kids are routinely tested even when not symptomatic, and then isolated if positive, then it should be done in most work places.

Otherwise the in-school transmissions we prevent will be drop in bucket of community transmissions

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias Maybe in the long run we can use rapid tests also for flu, and if you are actually infectious then you stay home. But we shouldn’t selectively enforce it for schools while everything else is open. Not just because it’s unfair but also because it’s pointless.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I think the Covid vaccine is actually more effective than the flu vaccine. Also masks do make a difference. If there is evidence that the risk from in-school infection is larger than community infection then isolation is worth it.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias Basically if new equilibrium is that large fraction of population will be exposed to Covid every year, might be better to focus on boosting&treatment rather than losing 5-10 days per exposure of school/work for people that feel fine.

(Though should first get through this wave.)

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias Most vaxxed+boosted kids and teachers that get Covid will have no or mild symptoms. It may well be that at the endemic phase, cost/benefit tradeoff is that positive people that feel well enough should still go to school/work (though maybe wear a mask).
